docs.title: Edge-Intelligent Health Monitoring over Adaptive Low-Power and Lossy Networks
docs.text:
A privacy-preserving wearable IoT mesh. Wrist-worn nodes measure heart rate, carry an embedded fall detector, and report over a self-organizing IEEE 802.15.4 / 6LoWPAN / RPL mesh built on RIOT OS. The site needs no cloud, and raw physiological data never leaves it.

Back to the project site View the code on GitHub

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: Elderly-care facilities, autism hostels and off-grid industrial sites need continuous monitoring of the people in them. These sites often have weak connectivity, and good reasons not to stream health data to a cloud service. A wearable that only talks to a single gateway also loses contact as soon as its wearer walks out of range.

docs.title: The approach
docs.text:
• On-node edge AI. A logistic-regression fall detector runs on the wearable's own IMU data, so only an alert has to cross the network.
  • Self-organizing mesh. Nodes join, leave and re-parent automatically over RPL, so a node out of the gateway's range is reached through other nodes.
  • Local only. One nRF52840 border-router dongle and a Raspberry Pi 4 on site are the entire infrastructure.
graph LR
    N1["HR node<br/>XIAO nRF52840 Sense<br/>IMU + MAX30102"] -- "802.15.4 / 6LoWPAN / RPL" --> N2["Relay node<br/>XIAO nRF52840 Sense"]
    N1 -. "direct when in range" .-> BR
    N2 --> BR["Border router<br/>nRF52840 dongle, RPL root"]
    BR -- "USB CDC-ECM" --> PI["Raspberry Pi 4<br/>sink, ACK, logging"]
    PI -- "ACK + seq" --> N1

docs.title: Key results
docs.text:
Area Result End-to-end Node → RPL mesh → border router → Pi 4 → ACK back to the node, with the RPL rank in every packet and packet loss tracked per node Range Link still up at about 55 m outdoors (50–60% loss), the farthest distance tested, at +8 dBm with on-board chip antennas Fall detection 94.9% of SisFall fall trials detected at a 9.8% ADL false-alarm rate (38 subjects, subject-wise nested CV) Footprint Fall model is 9 coefficients + intercept; node firmware is about 72 KB

Details on the Results page.

docs.title: Built with
docs.text:
Seeed XIAO nRF52840 Sense · MH-ET LIVE MAX30102 · Nordic PCA10059 · Raspberry Pi 4 · RIOT OS · Python / scikit-learn

M.Tech (Artificial Intelligence) thesis project by G Tanush Adithiya, supervised by Dr. M. Senthilkumar. Knowledge Engineering and Semantic Computing (KESC) research group, Amrita School of Computing, Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Coimbatore.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Component Role Seeed XIAO nRF52840 Sense ×N Wearable node: onboard LSM6DS3TR-C IMU + external MAX30102 PPG sensor, RIOT OS, custom RPL OF Nordic PCA10059 nRF52840 dongle Border router radio — runs RIOT gnrc_border_router, owns the RPL/6LoWPAN stack Raspberry Pi 4 Downstream host only — UDP server, logging, supervisor view. Does not run BR logic (RIOT has no slip-radio "dumb radio" path)

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
• IEEE 802.15.4 (O-QPSK, 250 kbps) at the PHY/MAC layer, 6LoWPAN for IPv6 header compression, RPL for mesh routing.
  • Wireless mesh prefix: 2001:db8::/64. BR uplink (to the Pi): 2001:db8:1::/64, static-configured (PREFIX_CONF=static), so the Pi side needs manual IPv6 address/route configuration — see docs/INSTALLATION.md.
  • Routing decisions (future work: custom OF) will weight a node's DODAG parent choice by its current health-urgency flag, residual battery, and IMU-derived mobility — a node mid-alert should get preferential routing over idle neighbors, not continuous ML-driven re-routing.

docs.title: On-device inference pipeline
docs.text:
1. Stage 1 — Fall detection (IMU, ML): 1–2 s accelerometer windows, 9 magnitude/tilt features, logistic regression classifier, running directly on the XIAO.
  2. Stage 2 — Severity check (PPG, rule-based): on a Stage-1 trigger, a 10–30 s heart-rate read determines whether the alert is "fall-only" or "critical."
  3. The combined alert level is what feeds the RPL routing priority above — this is deliberately not a continuous classifier driving routing on every packet.

docs.title: Software stack
docs.text:
• RIOT OS, custom apps built outside the RIOT tree (RIOTBASE pointing back at a pristine checkout — never edited in place).
  • MAX30102 driver written from scratch against RIOT's periph/i2c.h (no native driver exists in-tree).
  • Border router: stock RIOT gnrc_border_router example, UPLINK=cdc-ecm.
  • Pi 4: a plain Python UDP server (RIOT native board mode doesn't build on aarch64 — hardcoded x86 flags in RIOT's native board makefiles).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Linux dev machine (this project is developed on Fedora) with the ARM embedded GCC toolchain.
  • nrfutil — the Rust-based v8.x release (the legacy pip v5 release does not work for this dongle).
  • Python 3 on the Raspberry Pi 4.

docs.title: 1. RIOT OS + custom apps
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/RIOT-OS/RIOT.git ~/riotproject
# Custom apps live OUTSIDE the RIOT tree, pointing RIOTBASE back at it:
#   ~/riotproject-apps/<appname>/Makefile  ->  RIOTBASE ?= $(HOME)/riotproject

docs.title: 2. Flashing a XIAO node
docs.text:
Important: UF2_SOFTDEV=DROP must be passed on every flash. Without it the SoftDevice blocks the RIOT image, and once dropped, Arduino IDE / Nordic serial DFU will no longer work on that board — RIOT's UF2 drag-and-drop path is the only way to flash it from then on.

cd ~/riotproject-apps/<appname>
make BOARD=seeedstudio-xiao-nrf52840-sense UF2_SOFTDEV=DROP flash

If the board doesn't show up as a USB drive, double-tap reset to force the UF2 bootloader.

docs.title: 3. Border router
docs.text:
cd ~/riotproject/examples/networking/gnrc/gnrc_border_router
make BOARD=nrf52840dongle UPLINK=cdc-ecm PREFIX_CONF=static flash

gnrc_rpl must be enabled manually in the app's Makefile. Plug the flashed dongle into the Pi 4.

docs.title: 4. Raspberry Pi 4 side
docs.text:
PREFIX_CONF=static means the BR does not send router advertisements on its uplink, so the Pi's usb0 needs a persistent static config (survives dongle reconnects via systemd-networkd):

sudo tee /etc/systemd/network/10-usb0.network << 'NET'
[Match]
Name=usb0

[Network]
Address=2001:db8:1::2/64

[Route]
Destination=2001:db8::/64
Gateway=2001:db8:1::1
NET
sudo systemctl restart systemd-networkd
networkctl status usb0   # should show "routable (configured)"

Run the UDP server (see border-router/):

python3 ~/privacy-preserving-wearable/border-router/hr_reply_server.py

docs.title: 5. Verifying the mesh
docs.text:
On the border router shell (pyterm/serial over ttyACM0):

nib route     # confirm the node's route is present
nib neigh     # confirm a resolved neighbor entry

On the Pi 4, confirm traffic with tcpdump -i usb0 -n port 8888 while a node is sending.

docs.title: Fall detection (on-node edge AI)
docs.text: The detector is designed to run on the wearable, so only the resulting alert travels over the mesh. Today it is exported to C and verified against the Python reference on the host; validation on the band itself is the next step.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
graph LR
    A["LSM6DS3TR-C<br/>52 Hz, ±16 g"] --> B["2 s window<br/>(104 samples)"]
    B --> C["9 features<br/>magnitude + tilt"]
    C --> D["Logistic regression<br/>p ≥ 0.93"]
    D -- trigger --> E["3 s stillness check<br/>low motion, about 1 g"]
    E -- confirmed --> F["Fall alert"]
  1. Stage 1, IMU (machine learning): every 2 s window of accelerometer data is reduced to 9 features (magnitude statistics, jerk, low-g count, and the tilt change between before and after the impact) and scored by a logistic-regression model.
  2. Confirmation: a trigger only becomes an alert if the wearer then stays still for 3 s, as a person who has fallen typically does. This removes most false alarms from sitting down hard or similar movements.
  3. Stage 2, PPG (rule): a heart-rate check after the fall will classify the alert as critical or fall-only (future work).

docs.title: Why logistic regression
docs.text: Neural models (a TinyCNN on PPG data) did not reach the accuracy target. Classical models on hand-designed features did. Logistic regression gave the best recall/false-alarm trade-off at the trial level, and it fits on the node as 9 coefficients plus an intercept. The C export reproduces the Python model's output on every test vector.

docs.title: Training pipeline
docs.text:
Path Contents src/ Feature extraction (features.py, features_v2.py), training (train.py), evaluation (eval_*.py), C export (export_c.py, export_final.py) include/ Exported model headers and the feature spec, shared with the firmware-side copy results/ Metrics, sweep tables, nested-CV fold results, plots data/ Dataset notes (raw SisFall data and derived feature CSVs are gitignored — regenerate locally)

Dataset notes and rebuild steps: ml/fall-detection/data/README.md

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text: Physical build of the wearable node, the border router, and the enclosure.

docs.title: Bill of materials (per deployment)
docs.text: Qty Part Role 3 Seeed Studio XIAO nRF52840 Sense Wearable node MCU + IEEE 802.15.4 radio; on-board LSM6DS3TR-C IMU 3 MH-ET LIVE MAX30102 breakout PPG (red + IR) heart-rate sensor 3 3.7 V 250 mAh LiPo (502030) Node battery 3 SPST slide switch Inline power switch on the battery lead 1 Nordic PCA10059 nRF52840 USB dongle Border router radio / RPL root 1 Raspberry Pi 4 Downstream host: UDP sink, logging, supervisor view 3 3D-printed wrist enclosure + watch strap Node housing

docs.title: Wiring (wearable node)
docs.text:
MAX30102 XIAO nRF52840 Sense VIN 3V3 GND GND SDA / SCL I2C bus used by RIOT I2C_DEV(0)
  • Solder the 3V3 jumper on the back of the MH-ET LIVE MAX30102. Its I2C pull-ups default to the 1.8 V rail; with a 3.3 V host the sensor will not ACK (every read returns -ENXIO).
  • I2C addresses on the node bus: MAX30102 0x57, LSM6DS3TR-C 0x6B.
  • Use soldered joints or direct female–female jumpers. Breadboard contacts were unreliable for I2C in testing.

docs.title: Power
docs.text:
• The LiPo is soldered directly to the XIAO BAT+ / BAT− pads (no JST connector), with the slide switch inline on the positive lead. The XIAO charges the cell over USB-C.
  • Range and walk tests must run on battery. A USB-tethered node browns out and resets when the cable is tugged, which corrupts the measurement.

docs.title: Stack order (inside the case, skin side first)
docs.text:
1. MAX30102: bottom, sensor window facing the skin
  2. LiPo cell
  3. XIAO nRF52840 Sense: top
  4. Slide switch: on the side wall

docs.title: Enclosure
docs.text:
• Prototype 1 (HR node): 3D-printed box enclosure with hand-cut sensor and switch openings, using the spring-bar lug geometry from enclosure revision V1.3 (that lug gap fit standard watch straps well).
  • Nodes 2 and 3: redesign in progress, keeping the V1.3 lug/spring-bar geometry and the smaller V2 cavity. STL files will be added to hardware/enclosure/ as each revision is printed.

docs.title: RF notes
docs.text:
• Both the XIAO and the PCA10059 use small on-board chip antennas. External antennas were not used.
  • TX power is raised from RIOT's 0 dBm default to the nRF52840 maximum of +8 dBm on both nodes and the border router (firmware/mesh/rpl_tuning.mk).
  • 2.4 GHz is strongly attenuated by the body and by laptop chassis. For range tests, mount the node away from the body with clear line of sight.

docs.title: Mesh firmware
docs.text:
Source: firmware/mesh/

mesh/
├── rpl_tuning.mk        shared Trickle/lifetime/TX-power flags (every build includes it)
├── mesh_node/           ONE firmware for all XIAOs: make ROLE=hr | ROLE=relay
├── mesh_br/             nRF52840 dongle: border router + RPL root, auto-configured
└── server/mesh_server.py  Pi4 sink: per-node stats, replies "ACK"+seq

Built and checked against RIOT master (2026-11-12) with arm-none-eabi-gcc 13.2, -Werror: mesh_node hr 72 KB, relay 70 KB, mesh_br 98 KB.

docs.title: Install (Fedora)
docs.text:
cd <your repo clone> && git pull          # brings in firmware/mesh/
cd firmware/mesh
RIOTBASE defaults to ~/riotproject in both Makefiles, so the apps build from anywhere. Build output goes to bin/ (gitignored).

docs.title: Flash
docs.text:
# HR node (prototype 1, battery + MAX30102)  — double-tap reset for the UF2 drive
cd firmware/mesh/mesh_node
make ROLE=hr UF2_SOFTDEV=DROP flash

# the two relay XIAOs
make ROLE=relay UF2_SOFTDEV=DROP flash

# border router dongle: flash exactly the way you flashed gnrc_border_router before
cd ../mesh_br
make                     # -> bin/nrf52840dongle/mesh_br.hex for nrfutil
UF2_SOFTDEV=DROP is still mandatory on every XIAO flash.

Pi4: copy server/mesh_server.py over and run python3 mesh_server.py. It replaces hr_reply_server.py: the repo version of that script replies with a bare 3-byte ACK, while the firmware only accepts ACK+seq (7 bytes), and it mixed all nodes into one loss counter. The Pi4 usb0 systemd-networkd config stays as it is.

docs.title: What changed vs. the old apps
docs.text:
Problem Root cause (RIOT source) Fix nib prefix add 6 2001:db8:1::/64 after every BR boot gnrc_ipv6_static_addr adds the uplink address as a /128, so the /64 is never on-link mesh_br adds the prefix in main() ACKs dead after a BR reboot until rpl trickle reset Root always boots with the same version and DTSN=1, so nodes never resend DAOs and the BR has no downward routes Random DTSN at boot → every node resends its DAO; trickle reset at boot Nodes need a power-cycle to find a parent RIOT sends one DIS at init, then waits for DIOs; with Imax ≈ 2.3 h the wait can be hours DIS keeper thread: multicast DIS every 5 s while the node has no parent Slow reaction to moved/dead parents Imax 2.3 h, route lifetime 5 min Imax ≈ 33 s (Thread-like), 90 s routes, silent parent probed after 75 s MAX30102 FIFO overflow 500 ms blocking sock_udp_recv vs. a 320 ms FIFO ACKs handled in their own thread; FIFO polled every 100 ms; FIFO_OVF! flag if it ever happens

The power cost of the faster Trickle is negligible: the nRF52840 radio listens continuously anyway, and the HR node already transmits every 3 s, against one DIO every ~33 s.

docs.title: What you should see
docs.text:
HR node terminal: 

mesh_node role=HR period=3000ms sink=[2001:db8:1::2]:8888
[HR] MAX30102 OK (SpO2 mode, 100 Hz)
[RPL] no parent -> multicast DIS
[RPL] JOINED DODAG
[ADDR] 2001:db8::xxxx
[RPL] parent=fe80::... parent_rank=512 my_rank=768
[TX] seq=0 bpm=76 rank=768 hops=2 | loss=0% (0/0 ok) sent=1 acked=0 late=0
[ACK] seq=0 rtt=38ms
Relays print the same [RPL] lines plus a heartbeat [TX]/[ACK] every 10 s. BR on boot: 
[BR] uplink if 6: on-link prefix 2001:db8:1::/64 added
[BR] RPL root instance 0 dodag 2001:db8::... dtsn=137, trickle reset (Imin=1024ms, doublings=5)
Pi4: one [RX <node> HR|relay/hb] line per packet; type t + Enter for a per-node table, a number + Enter to tag the distance for walk tests (CSV: mesh_log.csv).

docs.title: Acceptance test — no shell commands allowed
docs.text:
Pass = the HR terminal shows [ACK] again within ~10 s (worst case ~40 s) of the last step, every time.

  1. BR + Pi4 up first, then power relay A, relay B, HR node.
  2. HR node first, then relays, BR last.
  3. Everything running → unplug/replug the BR dongle.
  4. HR node out of BR range so it hops through a relay → switch that relay off → it should re-parent through the other relay or the BR within ~2 min (silent-parent probe).
  5. Switch the relay back on → it rejoins on its own.

If a step fails, send me the HR, relay and BR terminal output from that step. rpl and nib route are still available on the BR shell for diagnosis.

docs.title: End-to-end communication
docs.text:
• Bidirectional path verified: node → RPL mesh → border router → Raspberry Pi 4 → ACK back to the node.
  • Every packet carries the node's sequence number, heart rate and current RPL rank. The Pi 4 sink tracks packet loss per node and per session, so loss counts stay correct across RPL rejoins.
  • Verified live against the border router's routing table and a tcpdump capture on the Pi 4.

docs.title: Radio range (single hop)
docs.text:
Two campaigns at 1 packet/s with server-side loss tracking, on-board chip antennas. Campaign A: clear line of sight, node USB-tethered to a laptop. Campaign B: outdoor open field. The two are not directly comparable.

Distance Packet loss 5 m (campaign A) about 4–5% 25 m (campaign A) about 13–17% about 55 m (campaign B, farthest distance tested) 50–60%

The link degrades gradually rather than failing suddenly. That makes multi-hop relaying through other wearers a better way to extend coverage than antenna modifications, which this form factor does not allow.

Lessons from field testing

  • A USB-tethered node browns out and resets when the cable is pulled, so the node now runs on its own battery.
  • At 2.4 GHz, a hand or the wearer's body, or a nearby laptop chassis, can cut the link completely. Mount the node away from both.

docs.title: Fall detection
docs.text:
Dataset: SisFall, 38 subjects (23 young, 15 elderly), 4505 trials, ADXL345 resampled to 52 Hz. Protocol: subject-wise 5-fold nested cross-validation. Thresholds are chosen on the inner folds only, and results are reported per trial.

Metric Value Fall trials detected (recall) 94.9% (1706 / 1798) ADL trials with a false alarm 9.8% (264 / 2702) ADL false-alarm rate, elderly subjects 2.9% Model size 9 coefficients + intercept

Raw sweep tables and per-fold results: ml/fall-detection/results/

docs.title: Future work
docs.text:
• Alert-priority routing: a custom RPL Objective Function in which only a node with an active alert changes parent selection
  • PPG severity stage after a detected fall
  • On-device validation with the XIAO's own recordings, and an own heart-rate dataset
  • Multi-node, multi-hop field evaluation and comparison with commercial wearables
